t: Check if Numbers Are Ascending in a Sentence - One Pass Over Tokens
o: Tokens are lowercase words or digit-only positive numbers separated by single spaces; we must confirm the numeric tokens, read left to right, increase strictly. In example 1 the numbers 1, 3, 4, 6, 12 rise strictly and the answer is true, while example 2 fails because 5 is followed by another 5 - equality violates the requirement. The sentence is short, and since numbers have no leading zeros and are positive, parsing is unambiguous and a "previous number" register can safely start at 0.
k: Compare numbers numerically, never as strings - "10" sorts before "9" lexicographically.
"Strictly increasing" rejects ties as well as decreases.
One scan with a last-seen-number register is enough.

a.i: Split the sentence on spaces, test whether each token starts with a digit, parse those tokens as integers, and compare each with the previously seen number. The most direct encoding of the statement.
s: For each digit-leading token, parse it; return false if it is <= prev.
Update prev and finish; return true if no violation appeared.
a.t: O(L) - each character of the sentence is touched a constant number of times (L = sentence length).

a.i: Walk the raw string with one pointer; whenever a digit starts a maximal digit run, parse that run in place and compare. This skips the token-array allocation and expresses the logic with pure index movement.
s: On a digit, consume the full run [i, j) while accumulating its numeric value.
Return false if the value is <= prev; otherwise record it and jump i to j.
Skip non-digit characters and return true at the end.
a.t: O(L) - a single pass with in-place digit parsing.

w: Even for an Easy, state the guarantees you exploit: positive numbers with no leading zeros justify starting prev at 0, and well-formed spacing makes splitting safe. The one real trap is comparing numeric tokens as strings ("10" < "9"); the second is forgetting that equal adjacent numbers fail. Natural follow-ups: check strictly decreasing order, support negative numbers or decimals, or process an unbounded token stream without buffering.
